turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You speak of his misfortunes, but what of the injustices you've perpetrated, Mr. Darcy? How do you expect me to forget your treatment of me and my family?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, truly astonished, that you would continue to harbor such bitter resentment towards me, after all I have done to make amends for my past mistakes.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I fail to see how your 'amends' have done anything to alleviate the hurt and insult you caused me. Your pride and arrogance still shine through, and I will not be swayed by empty words or shallow apologies.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Miss Elizabeth, that you should still harbor such unfounded resentment against me. Your refusal to consider my affections is a reflection of your own prejudices, rather than any fault of mine.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no prejudices, Mr. Darcy, only a clear-eyed understanding of your character and actions. Your interference in Bingley's relationship with Jane and your own condescending behavior towards me have left a lasting impression, and I will not be swayed by your romantic words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I am disappointed, though not surprised, by your rejection. Your opinion of me has been, shall we say, rather...influenced by my family's connections and my own pride.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no idea what you expect me to say to your declarations of love, Mr. Darcy. My opinion of you has been influenced by your own behavior, not just your family's connections. I find it rich that you're suddenly concerned about my feelings after years of treating me with disdain.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I am astonished by your continued animosity towards me, Elizabeth. Have you forgotten the esteem in which I hold you, and the sacrifices I have made for your benefit?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How dare you speak of esteem and sacrifices when your actions have shown me nothing but condescension and disdain for my own feelings and well-being?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Elizabeth, that you would so callously dismiss the ardent sentiments I have expressed, without even the courtesy of a consideration of my feelings.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You expect me to consider your feelings, Mr. Darcy, after the way you've treated me and my family? I think not.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: You wound me, Miss Bennet, with your words. I have done nothing to deserve such censure.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not censuring you, Mr. Darcy, I am simply stating the facts. Your behavior towards me has been condescending and dismissive, and I will not be swayed by grand declarations of love.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I fail to understand why you would so callously dismiss my affections, given the esteem in which I hold you, Elizabeth. Your rejection is a blow, to be sure, but I must confess that I had expected more generosity of spirit from one who has known me as intimately as you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must confess, Mr. Darcy, that I find it quite rich for you to speak of generosity of spirit, given your own behavior towards those you deem inferior. Your actions, not my rejection, are the true test of your character.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I assure you, Miss Bennet, that I am not one to be swayed by petty criticisms. Your own biases and prejudices have led you to misinterpret my actions, and I will not be lectured to by one who has so frequently maligned me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not one to be swayed by empty professions of love, Mr. Darcy. You have shown me time and time again that your words are not to be trusted.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I am astonished by your obstinacy in refusing my affections. Your rejection is a blow I had not anticipated, and I daresay, I find it quite... distressing.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I find it quite distressing that you're surprised by my rejection, considering the way you've treated me and my family in the past. Your pride and arrogance have always been an affront to me, and I see no reason to change my opinion now that you're professing love.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I expected as much from you. Your wounded pride and obstinacy have not diminished in the slightest, despite my declarations of love.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
